title: Northstar Fintech - Procurement + SLA language (Dedicated bounds: min baseline / max ceiling)
summary: Northstar and Redwood aligned on contract language for Dedicated autoscaling bounds: customer-configurable min baseline and hard max ceiling (spend control) enforced by the autoscaler, plus optional predictive scaling that cannot violate bounds. Legal/procurement asked for (1) explicit statement Redwood will not scale above max without written customer approval, (2) behavior/notifications when minimum cannot be met due to regional GPU shortage, (3) SLA measurement and service credits, and (4) auditability/RBAC around scaling policy changes. Redwood proposed wording that max is a hard invariant; min is a target with a defined degraded-state if capacity shortage occurs, with alerts + operational escalation and optional burst options. Next steps: Redwood to send redlines (SLA + Order Form exhibit) and a one-pager describing bounds semantics and audit log events; Northstar to confirm preferred baseline (min) and ceiling (max) for initial production region and whether predictive mode is required at launch.
topics: Dedicated order form: minimum baseline and maximum ceiling as contractual guardrails
Autoscaling semantics: bounds precedence vs platform defaults
Predictive scaling option and fallback to reactive
SLA definitions: availability, latency reporting, service credits
Region capacity shortage: unmet min behavior + comms
Audit logs, RBAC, change management for scaling policy updates
next_steps: Redwood (Naomi) to send proposed contract language for max-bound hard enforcement and predictive scaling semantics by 2025-08-07
Redwood (Lauren) to send a short technical appendix: scaling decision audit events + example payload fields by 2025-08-08
Northstar (Priyanka) to confirm initial bounds (min GPUs/replicas, max GPUs/replicas) for us-east-1 deployment and whether they want a separate staging deployment by 2025-08-11
Northstar Legal (Mark) to return redlines on shortage/unmet-min clause and service credit triggers by 2025-08-12
Schedule follow-up 30 min legal/procurement sync week of 2025-08-11
action_items: Naomi Feldman - Draft SLA + Order Form exhibit language: (a) max bound is hard invariant, (b) min bound is target with degraded-state definition + comms - Due 2025-08-07
Lauren Bishop - Provide product semantics one-pager: effective policy evaluation, precedence, predictive override rules, cooldowns, auditability - Due 2025-08-08
Marcus Lin - Confirm audit log retention and export options applicable to Northstar Dedicated - Due 2025-08-08
Priyanka Rao - Send Northstar's proposed baseline and ceiling numbers (and any time-of-day schedule expectations) - Due 2025-08-11
Mark Ellison - Review and propose edits to shortage/unmet-min language and whether 'commercially reasonable efforts' is acceptable - Due 2025-08-12
transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Title: Northstar Fintech - Procurement + SLA language (Dedicated bounds: min baseline / max ceiling)
Date: 2025-08-05
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes

Attendees
Redwood Inference: Liam O'Rourke, Lauren Bishop, Naomi Feldman, Marcus Lin
Northstar Fintech: Ava Chen, Mark Ellison, Priyanka Rao, Jorge Alvarez

---

[00:00] Liam O'Rourke: Cool, thanks everyone. I think this is the last leg before we get to signature, hopefully. Today is mostly procurement slash legal, specifically the SLA and the scaling bounds language. Lauren and Naomi are here in case we need to get precise on product semantics.

[00:16] Ava Chen: Yep, thanks Liam. We can keep it tight. Mark and I want to make sure the paper matches what Priyanka heard on the technical deep dive.

[00:25] Priyanka Rao: Yeah. The big thing for us is the min baseline and the max ceiling. We need it to be enforceable, not "best effort".

[00:34] Lauren Bishop: Understood. And just to frame: max is enforced as a hard clamp in the autoscaler. Min is also enforced as a floor in the policy evaluation, but there are physical constraints like region capacity shortage. We can define how we report it and what remedies are.

[00:52] Mark Ellison: Right, that's the nuance. If you say "never below min" but then you can't provision, that's a potential breach. We need contract language that is truthful and gives us options.

[01:03] Naomi Feldman: Makes sense. We typically handle that with a concept of "Committed Capacity" vs "Requested Minimum". For Dedicated reserved pools we can structure a baseline commitment, and then allow the min autoscaling policy to be at or below that. For above committed, we can define as "burst" and best efforts.

[01:21] Jorge Alvarez: Just to jump in, from finance, the ceiling is actually the scarier part. We had an incident with another vendor where a scaling bug basically doubled spend.

[01:31] Ava Chen: Exactly. We need a hard cap that you cannot exceed unless we approve.

[01:36] Liam O'Rourke: Yep. That aligns with why we built the feature. The hard max bound is a spend guardrail, enforced by the fleet autoscaler. Even if reactive signals scream, it won't exceed the max.

[01:49] Mark Ellison: When you say "won't exceed", I want that in the contract. Like: "Provider shall not increase provisioned GPUs above Customer-specified maximum".

[02:00] Naomi Feldman: We can propose language like: "Redwood will not scale the Dedicated Deployment above the Maximum Capacity setting configured by Customer in the Console/API, except with Customer's written authorization." Then we can add a sentence clarifying Customer controls that config and changes are audited.

[02:18] Priyanka Rao: That would work. But the next question is: who counts as "Customer" for written authorization? We need it to be a role, not a random engineer.

[02:28] Marcus Lin: On the product side we have RBAC for who can edit scaling policies. For enterprise we can limit to Admins, and we can also log every config change with who/when/what. If you want it to map to a contract concept, we can reference "Customer Authorized Users".

[02:45] Mark Ellison: Good. So for authorization, we can say "Authorized Representative" or similar.

[02:53] Ava Chen: Also, I want clarity on billing. If max is, say, 40 GPUs, are we charged for 40 even if it's not used?

[03:02] Liam O'Rourke: For Dedicated, you typically commit to a reserved baseline pool. Then autoscaling happens within that pool plus any agreed burst capacity. The min/max bounds in the product are about how many replicas / GPUs the autoscaler targets at runtime. Billing depends on the committed pool and any burst usage as defined in the Order Form.

[03:22] Jorge Alvarez: So we'd set committed maybe 24, min maybe 24, max maybe 40, and you don't charge the delta unless we burst?

[03:30] Liam O'Rourke: Correct, assuming the Order Form defines burst as metered. We can confirm the commercial structure, but that's the typical.

[03:40] Ava Chen: Okay. Mark, your main thing is the SLA and remedies.

[03:44] Mark Ellison: Yeah. Two things. One, availability SLA. Two, performance/latency. I know you don't promise p95 under all loads, but you did show dashboards.

[03:55] Lauren Bishop: For Dedicated we can share typical latency SLO targets, but contractually we usually stick to availability plus support response. That said, we can add an operational commitment around scaling bounds and notification when you're hitting max.

[04:10] Priyanka Rao: We do need some performance assurances though. Our app is real-time-ish, and the predictable ramp is exactly why we want predictive scaling.

[04:18] Liam O'Rourke: Right. What we've done with other fintechs is: contract SLA is uptime; then we attach a Technical Exhibit that defines scaling behavior and observability metrics, plus escalation. It becomes enforceable via the support process rather than credits.

[04:34] Mark Ellison: I may accept that, but I want clear triggers for "you're at max and queue is building" because otherwise it's finger pointing.

[04:44] Lauren Bishop: Totally. In the product we now have metrics like desired replicas vs bounded replicas and a "max-bound hit" counter, plus queue depth. We can commit to providing those dashboards.

[04:58] Marcus Lin: And audit logs for decisions: requested desired, bounded desired, and the reason. That's important for postmortems.

[05:07] Ava Chen: Wait, audit logs for "decisions" too? Or just config changes.

[05:12] Marcus Lin: Both. Config changes: who changed min/max, predictive toggle, cooldowns. Scaling decisions: the autoscaler emits an event that includes the evaluated desired number, the bounded number, and the reason it clamped.

[05:28] Mark Ellison: Is that retained? Can we export to our SIEM?

[05:33] Marcus Lin: Retention depends on package; for enterprise we can do longer retention and export. I want to double-check the exact durations before I promise a number on the call.

[05:44] Naomi Feldman: We can write in that logs are available and exportable subject to the product plan / Order Form. And then specify the retention in the Order Form.

[05:56] Priyanka Rao: On predictive scaling, I want to make sure it's not going to violate max. That was our worry in the pilot story you told us.

[06:05] Lauren Bishop: Correct. Predictive can only influence the "requested desired". Then we clamp to bounds. Even if prediction is wrong, reactive signals can override prediction to scale up faster, but still cannot exceed max.

[06:20] Priyanka Rao: And scale down won't go below min.

[06:23] Lauren Bishop: Exactly. Plus we have cooldowns and anti-oscillation dampening.

[06:29] Mark Ellison: Let's get to the tricky clause: if you can't meet the minimum.

[06:34] Naomi Feldman: Yep. So, proposed approach: define "Minimum Capacity" as a configured setting. Redwood will attempt to maintain it, but if there is a regional capacity shortage, Redwood will (a) notify within X minutes, (b) mark the deployment in degraded state, (c) work to restore, and (d) provide service credits if the shortage causes an availability breach.

[06:58] Mark Ellison: If you call it "minimum" in contract, it reads like a guarantee. I'd rather call it "Baseline" or "Floor" and add "subject to capacity".

[07:09] Priyanka Rao: But we don't want "subject to" to be a loophole.

[07:13] Jorge Alvarez: Yeah, because then what's the point.

[07:16] Liam O'Rourke: What we can do commercially is: you reserve a baseline pool (committed) that we guarantee is allocated to you in that region. Then the "min" in the product equals that committed baseline. In that case, it's not "subject to" except extreme force majeure.

[07:33] Ava Chen: That sounds more like what we want.

[07:36] Mark Ellison: If you can guarantee that baseline in the region, put it in the Order Form as committed capacity.

[07:43] Naomi Feldman: Yes. We'll align contract terms: committed capacity is a commercial commitment. The scaling policy min setting should not exceed that committed amount unless you choose to rely on burst.

[07:56] Priyanka Rao: For our initial rollout, we were thinking 24 GPUs baseline, 40 cap. But we may need 48 during quarter-end.

[08:05] Jorge Alvarez: Quarter-end is a known event. That's where predictive scaling helps but also we might temporarily raise max.

[08:13] Liam O'Rourke: Exactly. Predictive doesn't create new capacity beyond your max; it just gets you there earlier. For quarter-end, we can plan a temporary max increase with your approval, or add a scheduled event on our side, depending on what you prefer.

[08:27] Mark Ellison: Let's write into the contract that max changes require approval.

[08:31] Marcus Lin: Product-wise, max changes are just a config update, but we can enforce RBAC and also rate-limit config changes to prevent churn. If you want "approval" to be a process, we can add an admin-only requirement plus audit.

[08:48] Ava Chen: The approval process for us is: Priyanka or me. Not an engineer.

[08:53] Priyanka Rao: Yes.

[08:55] Naomi Feldman: Then in the Order Form we can identify who is the "Authorized Contact" for capacity changes, and we can also reflect that in RBAC instructions.

[09:06] Mark Ellison: Another clause: "Provider will not exceed maximum" should include "including due to errors or bugs".

[09:14] Lauren Bishop: The system enforces it at the autoscaler evaluation step. So even if there is a prediction glitch, it clamps. We also added a hotfix earlier when predictor returned null and we ensured we never scale to zero. So yes, the intent is: bugs shouldn't break the invariant.

[09:31] Mark Ellison: Intent is fine. Contract language should be "shall not".

[09:35] Naomi Feldman: We can do "shall not" for max. For min, I would do "will use commercially reasonable efforts" unless it's committed baseline.

[09:47] Ava Chen: Can we separate "Committed Baseline" and "Configured Min"? Because Priyanka wants the tool setting, but we want the contract anchor.

[09:56] Naomi Feldman: Yes. That's clean. Committed Baseline is contractual. Configured Min is operational and cannot exceed Committed Baseline unless you choose Burst mode.

[10:09] Priyanka Rao: Operationally, can it actually prevent me from setting min above committed? Like validation?

[10:15] Lauren Bishop: We can add validation in Console: if you try to set min above committed, we either block or warn depending on account settings. For enterprise we can block.

[10:27] Priyanka Rao: Block is good.

[10:29] Liam O'Rourke: Great. Let's capture that.

[10:33] Mark Ellison: On SLA credits, what are you offering? Standard 99.9 with credit tiers?

[10:41] Naomi Feldman: Standard for Dedicated is 99.9% monthly availability, measured at the API endpoint for your dedicated deployment. Credits tier based on downtime minutes. I can send the exact schedule.

[10:55] Mark Ellison: We will likely ask for 99.95. It's fintech.

[10:59] Liam O'Rourke: That may come with premium SLA add-on. Let's not negotiate numbers live, but we can take it back.

[11:07] Jorge Alvarez: If we pay premium, okay, but then max cap is even more important.

[11:12] Lauren Bishop: Another thing to clarify: if you hit max and performance degrades, that's not downtime. But we can build operational alerts and a runbook.

[11:23] Priyanka Rao: We also want some routing fallback, like if Dedicated is saturated, can we spill to hosted? But I think that's out of scope.

[11:31] Liam O'Rourke: It's an option, but not part of this contract. We can discuss separately.

[11:37] Ava Chen: Let's stick to what's needed to sign.

[11:40] Mark Ellison: Okay. I want the following in an exhibit:
1) Definitions of min and max settings.
2) Statement max is hard enforced.
3) Predictive mode cannot violate max.
4) Notifications when max is reached and queue is building.
5) Audit logs for changes.

[12:02] Naomi Feldman: Great. We'll draft that.

[12:05] Marcus Lin: On notifications, we can commit to alerts in the Console and optionally email/webhook to your on-call.

[12:13] Priyanka Rao: Webhook would be ideal.

[12:16] Lauren Bishop: We have that on the roadmap; today we have alerting via Grafana/PagerDuty integration for enterprise accounts, not direct webhooks. We should not promise a webhook unless we know.

[12:28] Liam O'Rourke: Correct, let's be careful. We can say "alerts available" and specify integration method in the implementation plan.

[12:36] Ava Chen: Great.

[12:38] Mark Ellison: How do you prevent someone from quickly toggling the bounds and causing issues? Like configuration churn.

[12:45] Marcus Lin: There's rate limiting on policy updates. If someone tries to change bounds repeatedly, we throttle and emit an audit event. Also, changes require admin permission.

[12:58] Mark Ellison: Good. Put that in the exhibit.

[13:02] Naomi Feldman: We'll include "controls to prevent configuration churn" but keep it high-level.

[13:08] Priyanka Rao: I also want the precedence spelled out. Like if platform default wants to scale beyond max, it won't. And if prediction suggests lower than reactive needs, reactive wins, but still respects min/max.

[13:23] Lauren Bishop: Exactly. Precedence is: compute desired from signals (reactive and optionally predictive). Then apply safety guardrails like cooldown/step. Then clamp to [min,max]. Then output bounded desired. And we log both.

[13:40] Priyanka Rao: Perfect.

[13:42] Ava Chen: Mark, any other legal gotchas.

[13:45] Mark Ellison: Data and logs. If audit logs are in scope, they may contain identifiers. We need standard security posture: encryption, access controls.

[13:54] Marcus Lin: Yes. Audit logs are in our standard logging pipeline, encrypted at rest, access controlled, SOC 2 controls. For Dedicated, we can restrict access further and provide exports. Again, retention and export methods per Order Form.

[14:09] Mark Ellison: Okay.

[14:11] Jorge Alvarez: One more money thing. If we set max at 40 and we hit it every day at 3pm, we're going to get queueing unless we raise the max. Predictive won't help if max is too low.

[14:23] Lauren Bishop: Correct. Predictive helps you avoid cold starts and avoid being late to scale, but it can't break physics. If max is too low for peak traffic, you'll saturate.

[14:34] Priyanka Rao: That's fine. The max is a budget lever. If we choose a low max, we accept some performance degradation. But we need it visible.

[14:43] Liam O'Rourke: And we can set up a "max-bound saturation" alert so you know it's happening.

[14:49] Ava Chen: That's a good point. If we choose the cap, it is on us. But we need transparency.

[14:57] Mark Ellison: Yep, transparency language is fine.

[15:01] Naomi Feldman: So the exhibit can also note: "If Customer-configured Maximum Capacity is reached, performance may degrade and requests may queue; Redwood will provide visibility via metrics and alerts." That avoids a dispute later.

[15:17] Mark Ellison: Great.

[15:19] Liam O'Rourke: Can we talk about the specific numbers now? Or do you want that offline.

[15:24] Priyanka Rao: We can share tentative. We think baseline 24 GPUs A100 equivalent in us-east-1, max 40. For quarter-end, maybe 48 max for 5 days.

[15:37] Jorge Alvarez: If the burst pricing is okay.

[15:40] Ava Chen: We'll want that in the Order Form: baseline and a burst cap.

[15:45] Liam O'Rourke: Understood. We'll propose: committed baseline 24, burst up to 48 with metering, and operational max default 40 unless you approve an event.

[15:58] Mark Ellison: Careful: operational max and burst cap might conflict. If burst cap is 48 but operational max is 40, you can burst but you won't.

[16:07] Lauren Bishop: Right. You'd need to change max to use burst. The contract can define burst eligibility; the product setting controls actual scaling.

[16:18] Priyanka Rao: That's fine. We'll raise max for quarter-end with an approval.

[16:24] Ava Chen: I'd like a simple process: email approval, then Redwood applies it.

[16:29] Liam O'Rourke: We can do either: you apply it in Console as admin, or Redwood does it for you via support request. If you prefer email approval, Redwood support can apply.

[16:42] Mark Ellison: And that should be documented.

[16:45] Naomi Feldman: We'll add to the exhibit: "Capacity setting changes may be made by Customer admin users in Console or by Redwood upon verified request from Authorized Contacts."

[16:57] Marcus Lin: And it will show up in audit logs either way.

[17:01] Priyanka Rao: Great.

[17:03] Mark Ellison: Switching gears: predictive mode. Is it GA? Or beta. We need to know what we're committing to.

[17:10] Lauren Bishop: It's in controlled rollout today, enabled per account. For your timeline, we can include it as a contracted feature with an enablement date, or we can treat it as optional. But the core need—hard bounds—can ship first. Predictive can follow.

[17:28] Priyanka Rao: Our ramp issue is real. I would like predictive for day one, but if the bounds is day one and predictive is within, say, a month, we can handle with manual schedule.

[17:39] Liam O'Rourke: Makes sense. We can write a statement in the implementation plan: predictive scaling to be enabled during onboarding, subject to readiness review. But I'd rather not put a hard date in the MSA.

[17:54] Ava Chen: We'll accept it in the onboarding plan, not as legal obligation.

[17:58] Mark Ellison: As long as the bounds are legally binding.

[18:02] Naomi Feldman: Yes.

[18:04] (crosstalk)

[18:06] Jorge Alvarez: One more question: If you can't meet the baseline due to shortage, do we get credits even if uptime is fine but latency suffers?

[18:17] Naomi Feldman: Credits typically apply to availability SLA. Latency issues don't automatically trigger credits. But we can define escalation and potentially commercial remedies if it's severe.

[18:29] Mark Ellison: We'll likely push for a "capacity shortfall" remedy.

[18:34] Liam O'Rourke: Let's take that offline. What we can do is: if committed baseline is not delivered, that is arguably a breach of the Order Form, and we can include a credit. But we need to ensure we can meet it.

[18:49] Lauren Bishop: Operationally, if committed baseline is guaranteed, shortage shouldn't happen. If it does, it's an incident.

[18:57] Priyanka Rao: Exactly. If we pay for baseline and don't get it, that's a problem.

[19:03] Naomi Feldman: Okay. We'll propose a clause: failure to provide committed baseline for more than X minutes constitutes downtime for SLA purposes. We'll confirm with leadership.

[19:18] Mark Ellison: Great. That's the kind of clarity we need.

[19:22] Ava Chen: Okay. What about audit logs: do you have a standard list of events?

[19:27] Marcus Lin: Standard events include: scaling_policy.updated, scaling_policy.validation_failed, autoscaler.decision, autoscaler.clamped_by_bound, min_unmet_due_to_shortage. Names may differ slightly but that's the idea.

[19:44] Priyanka Rao: I'd love to see an example payload, even if anonymized.

[19:48] Lauren Bishop: We can provide a sample with fields like deployment_id, region, requested_desired, bounded_desired, min, max, signals used, prediction_age. We'll keep it stable.

[20:05] Mark Ellison: Great.

[20:07] Ava Chen: Time check. We have like 10 minutes.

[20:10] Liam O'Rourke: Cool, let's recap what we'll send.

[20:14] Liam O'Rourke: Naomi will send draft redlines for the MSA/SLA and an exhibit with the bounds semantics. Lauren will send a one-pager on the product behavior, including precedence and audit logs. Marcus will confirm retention/export options.

[20:28] Ava Chen: And we'll respond with preferred numbers and redlines.

[20:31] Priyanka Rao: I'll confirm baseline 24, max 40 initial, plus burst to 48. Also, any timezone stuff—predictive should be aligned to our business day.

[20:43] Lauren Bishop: Yes, predictive uses the deployment region timezone unless configured. We'll cover that.

[20:49] Mark Ellison: Great. If you can get us redlines by Thursday, we can keep signature on track for next week.

[20:57] Liam O'Rourke: That's the plan.

[21:00] Ava Chen: Thanks everyone.

[21:02] (meeting ends)
